To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

patients with panic disorder show aberrant neural activity to disorder‐related stimuli compared to healthy controls in an extended fear circuitry, including brainstem, insular cortex, thalamus and anterior cingulate cortex.

patients with panic disorder show increased neural activation in a fear network comprising brain stem, insula, anterior cingulate cortex, thalamus and medial prefrontal cortex in response to disorder‐related versus matched neutral visual scenes.
the neural correlates of anxiety evoked by disorder‐related stimuli are directly related to altered brainstem activation and subjective anxiety levels in panic disorder.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobiology of panic disorder, a severe anxiety disorder that is characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks.
the study of anxiety disorders and the neural underpings thereof.
understanding the brain mechanisms of anxiety disorders, and in particular the mechanisms underlying the pathological fear and anxiety that are the core symptoms of these disorders.
